original_summary: Framton Nuttel, a nervous young man sent to the country to rest his nerves, makes a polite call on Mrs. Sappleton with a letter of introduction from his sister. While he waits, her fifteen-year-old niece Vera tells him a sad story: three years ago to the day, her aunt's husband and two young brothers went out shooting through the big open window, were swallowed by a bog, and never came back, and the aunt still leaves the window open every evening, believing they will return. When Mrs. Sappleton comes in, she cheerfully says her husband and brothers will be home soon, and Framton, horrified, tries in vain to talk about his illness. At dusk, she sees three figures with guns and a spaniel crossing the lawn, and a young voice sings the line that Vera had quoted. Framton runs out in terror. The men walk in, ordinary and muddy, and Vera calmly explains that Mr. Nuttel must have been frightened by the dog, adding an invented story about his past. The narrator ends with one line: romance at short notice was her speciality.
seed_elements: A self-possessed fifteen-year-old girl keeps a nervous visitor company while her aunt is late, and the visitor, who has come only to deliver a letter of introduction for his nerve cure, knows nothing about the household.

The girl tells him a calm, tragic tale about the large French window left open: three years ago to the day, the aunt's husband and two young brothers walked out through it to go shooting and were lost in a bog, their bodies never found, and the aunt still waits for them every evening.

The girl's story is built on small convincing details (the husband's white waterproof coat, the youngest brother singing 'Bertie, why do you bound?' to tease his sister, the little brown spaniel) and a sudden break in her voice, which makes the visitor believe her and makes the open window feel eerie.

The aunt then enters, cheerful and busy, speaks of the men coming home any moment, keeps looking toward the open window, and barely listens to the visitor's long talk about his illness, so everything she does seems to confirm the girl's story.

At twilight, three figures with guns, one with a white coat over his shoulders and a tired brown spaniel at their heels, walk silently across the lawn toward the window; then a young voice chants 'I said, Bertie, why do you bound?' and the terrified visitor flees past a cyclist on the road.

The men come in, ordinary and muddy; the aunt says the visitor must have seen a ghost, and the girl calmly says he was afraid of the spaniel, backing it up with a vivid invented tale about his past; the story ends with the narrator's own last line ("Romance at short notice was her speciality."), which shows that the girl invents stories on the spur of the moment.
discarded_elements: Most of the visitor's sister's advice and the detailed description of his nerve cure
Details such as snipe, duck, the scarcity of birds, and the muddy carpets that only decorate the aunt's chatter
The cyclist who nearly collides with the fleeing visitor, if space is needed

Names of minor people other than the visitor and the girl (the aunt's name, the brothers' names), if a shorter version works better with roles such as her aunt, the aunt's husband and her two brothers
Extended narration of the visitor's inner thoughts about letters of introduction and strangers
conversion_plan: Keep the English country house setting and the original order of events; do not modernize the setting. Write it mainly in natural third-person English at about 400 words, with a nervous visitor (Framton Nuttel) as the main character and role descriptions such as the girl (the niece), her aunt, the aunt's husband and her two brothers for the other people. Preserve the central story, the relationships between the characters, the cause-and-effect chain and the ending: the girl's calm ghost story about the open window; the aunt's cheerful behavior that seems to confirm it; the three figures appearing in the twilight and the familiar song; the visitor running away in panic; the girl's smooth lie about the dog, which reveals that she made up the whole tragedy; and the narrator's own one-line last sentence of the original, that romance at short notice was her speciality. Keep the suspense of the moment the figures appear and keep the dry humor of the final lie. Do not explain the trick, hint that the girl is lying, or comment on the twist before the ending, and do not add a moral or an explanation of your own after the last line. The original's own final sentence is not such an explanation: it is the closing line of the story and must be kept; the surprise is the point. Compress by trimming the visitor's background and the aunt's small talk, not by cutting the foreshadowing about the open window.

title: 開いた窓 The Open Window (Saki)

ending_reveal.meaning: The story ends by showing that the girl, Vera, is someone who invents convincing stories on the spur of the moment: her last smooth lie about why Framton ran away proves that her tragic ghost story was invented too.
ending_reveal.source_quote: Romance at short notice was her speciality.
ending_reveal.withhold_until_end: Before the ending, do not hint at or explain that Vera's story about the open window is invented.

setups_and_payoffs.setup: Vera's sad story: three years ago the aunt's husband and her two young brothers walked out through the open window and were lost in a bog; the aunt still keeps the window open; details are the husband's white coat, the youngest brother's song 'Bertie, why do you bound?' and the brown spaniel.
setups_and_payoffs.payoff: At dusk three figures with guns, a white coat and a spaniel cross the lawn and the song is heard; Framton runs away in terror; the men walk in, ordinary and muddy.

key_roles.name: Framton
key_roles.role: the nervous visitor and main character, who flees in terror

key_roles.name: Vera
key_roles.role: the aunt's fifteen-year-old niece, who tells the false ghost story and then lies smoothly about the dog
the girl's aunt, whose cheerful waiting for the men seems to confirm Vera's story

key_causality: Vera's invented tragedy makes Framton believe the men are ghosts; the aunt's cheerful behavior seems to confirm it; the men's return makes Framton flee in terror; Vera then invents another story to explain why he ran.
free_to_cut: the sister's advice and the nerve-cure details, the shooting-trip small talk, the cyclist, and most of Framton's inner thoughts
source_essentials.narration_voice: The story is told in the third person by an outside narrator, close on Framton, in a cool, dry, matter-of-fact voice that plays the events straight.
